Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
There is something wrong with me as a person
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette: Saravanan, a 40-year-old South Eastern Asian journalist, has been struggling with the aftermath of torture he endured in his home country before seeking asylum in America. The traumatic event itself was both visceral and indelible: Saravanan had been captured by agents who accused him of reporting information that incriminated high-ranking officials. Held for weeks, he experienced intense physical and psychological abuse. Despite his survival and eventual escape to the United States, the memories persistently haunt him. Since arriving in America, Saravanan has noticed how specific triggers bring back fragments of those traumatic experiences. The sound of children crying is particularly distressing; it reminds him of the screams of prisoners who were similarly tortured and held in nearby cells. This auditory trigger often leads to dizziness or lightheadedness, as he relives the intense panic and fear of his past ordeal. He also feels that hearing certain names related to his captors can evoke a similar visceral response. Saravanan’s coping strategies are deeply rooted in these triggers. He has started avoiding social contacts, seeing people from before the traumatic event because they remind him of his former life and the vulnerability he felt. This avoidance is compounded by his habit of undereating as a way to manage his anxiety and emotions. The thought of reliving those moments through interactions with others is overwhelming, leading him to isolate himself further. His constant dwelling on how the event could have been prevented also contributes significantly to his psychological distress. He often ruminates over whether he could have done something differently to avoid capture or if reporting less controversial stories would have spared him from torture. This rumination exacerbates his negative emotions of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. Saravanan’s sense of being watched by others for signs that they might harm him is a persistent threat that he carries with him daily. He starts at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, believing that any sudden noise could signal danger. This hyper-vigilance is tied to his belief that the trauma he endured was so extreme and real that it feels like it didn’t happen to him, making it difficult for him to fully recall or process what happened. The memory of the event itself is fragmented; there are parts he simply cannot remember no matter how hard he tries. This difficulty in recalling specific details leads him to believe that others can see the trauma etched on his face and that there must be something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. He feels violated by the acts committed against him, believing they go against who he is and what he stands for. These negative appraisals fuel his maladaptive coping strategies further. The belief that he has been exposed to others in such a way that they can see through him leads him to avoid social contacts entirely. His undereating becomes more pronounced as he tries to numb the emotional pain of these self-perceived defects and violations. This cycle of negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and memory difficulties reinforces his sense of threat and isolation. Saravanan’s occupation as a journalist exacerbates this situation. In his line of work, interacting with people is crucial, but he finds it increasingly difficult to engage in conversations or attend events without feeling the weight of past trauma. This avoidance has led him to miss important networking opportunities and even deadlines at times, affecting his professional life. What finally brought Saravanan to seek help was a combination of these mounting issues: his inability to fully function at work due to overwhelming anxiety, a growing sense of isolation from friends and family, and the realization that he could no longer ignore the impact of the trauma on his daily life. He is most afraid of being trapped in this cycle of fear and avoidance forever but also hopes for a way to reclaim his identity and find peace with his past without it controlling his present.
